title: The ontological argument
note: Ontological arguments reason from the concept of God alone. Anselm defines God as that than which nothing greater can be conceived and argues that such a being must exist in reality, not only in the mind. Critics attack the step from concept to existence; modal versions shift the weight onto one premise: that God's existence is possible.

read.title: Anselm's argument and the island
text: In Proslogion II, Anselm answers the fool of the Psalms, who says in his heart that there is no God. Even the fool understands the phrase 'a being than which nothing greater can be conceived.' Anselm's argument can be set out as a reductio:

(1) God is that than which nothing greater can be conceived. (2) God exists at least in the understanding. (3) Existing in reality as well as in the understanding is greater than existing in the understanding alone. (4) Suppose God existed in the understanding alone. (5) Then a greater being could be conceived: one that also exists in reality. (6) But nothing greater than God can be conceived. (7) Therefore God exists in reality.

The monk Gaunilo replied with a parody. Imagine an island more excellent than all other lands. By the same steps, it must exist, since an island that exists is more excellent than one that does not. Since that conclusion is absurd, something in the method must be wrong.

Anselm answered that his reasoning applies only to the being than which nothing greater can be conceived, not to the greatest member of a limited kind. Plantinga later sharpened the reply: the qualities that make an island great, such as beaches, have no intrinsic maximum, so 'the greatest possible island' is incoherent. Power, knowledge, and goodness, by contrast, do have maximal degrees.
Kant's objection goes deeper. Existence, he argued, is not a real predicate: it adds nothing to a concept, so no concept, however rich, can contain a guarantee of its own instance.

q.q: Which step does the reductio suppose in order to refute it?
o: That God exists in the understanding alone

q.q: How does Plantinga answer the island parody?
o: Islands are too small to matter
Island greatness has no intrinsic maximum
Islands exist only in the mind
The fool does not understand the phrase
Existence is not a real predicate that a concept can contain
